Physical signs of severe AS include a slow-rising pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus), an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, and a soft or absent A2 component of S2.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose severe aortic stenosis from classic physical examination findings (slow-rising pulse, murmur radiating to carotids).

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Severe aortic stenosis is defined echocardiographically by a peak aortic velocity (Vmax) >= 4.0 m/s, a mean transvalvular gradient >= 40 mmHg, and an aortic valve area (AVA) < 1.0 cm2 (or indexed AVA < 0.6 cm2/m2). With Vmax 4.3 m/s, mean gradient 44 mmHg, and AVA 0.8 cm2, this patient meets all hemodynamic criteria for severe aortic stenosis.
questions.learning_objective: Apply echocardiographic criteria (Vmax >4 m/s, mean gradient >40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm2) to define severe aortic stenosis.
questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with exertional angina undergoes transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for evaluation of a systolic murmur. The calculated aortic valve area by the continuity equation is 0.8 cm2 (indexed AVA 0.45 cm2/m2). Left ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. According to international and UK NICE NG208 criteria, how should the severity of her aortic stenosis be classified?

questions.explanation: Multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) is the reference technique for pre-procedural planning of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI/TAVR). It provides precise three-dimensional measurements of the aortic valve annulus, coronary ostial heights, calcification distribution, and evaluation of peripheral iliofemoral vascular access routes. Exercise stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS.
questions.learning_objective: Identify multidetector CT as the reference imaging technique for pre-procedural TAVI anatomical evaluation.

questions.explanation: In functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation (FMR), the mitral valve leaflets and chordae tendineae are structurally normal. The regurgitation is driven by left ventricular remodeling, annular dilatation, and papillary muscle displacement that cause apical and lateral leaflet tethering. In contrast, primary (degenerative) MR involves intrinsic structural leaflet/chordal disease (e.g. myxomatous degeneration, flail leaflet, or chordal rupture).
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the pathophysiology of functional mitral regurgitation (LV remodelling) from primary degenerative mitral disease.

citations.quote: Objectives: The optimal surgical approach for the treatment of functional mitral regurgitation (FMR) remains controversial. Current guidelines suggest that the surgical approach has to be tailored to the individual patient.

questions.explanation: In functional mitral regurgitation (FMR), guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (including ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2i, plus cardiac resynchronization therapy if indicated) is the essential first-line foundation. Optimal medical therapy promotes reverse LV remodeling and can substantially diminish the severity of functional regurgitation. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) or surgery is considered only if severe symptomatic MR persists despite optimal GDMT.
questions.learning_objective: Identify guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure as the mandatory initial management for functional mitral regurgitation.

questions.explanation: The major limitation of restrictive mitral valve annuloplasty repair in functional mitral regurgitation is a significant rate of recurrent mitral regurgitation (observed in up to 30–50% of patients within 2 years in randomized CTSN trials), primarily driven by ongoing left ventricular remodeling and progressive leaflet tethering. Despite this risk, repair avoids prosthetic valve-related complications and has been associated with favorable operative recovery in selected cohorts.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize recurrent mitral regurgitation as the primary long-term challenge of annuloplasty repair in functional MR.
